story_text.value:
Hi HN,

Trying to keep up to date, I am subscribed to Lenny's Newsletter, Nate's Substack, Simon Sinek, ByteByteGo, This Week in AI, you get the point. And I read almost none of it, because it lands in Gmail between receipts and work threads, and the inbox is the worst place I know to read anything long.

What I actually wanted was to read it on my Kindle, the way I read books. The project started out as "rssInk": RSS plus eInk. Then I ran into paid subscriptions, and the fact that I was actually consuming email not RSS so it became Newsstand.

It gives you a private address. I set up a Gmail filter that forwards my newsletters there, and now they show up like a morning paper: a section per publication, the ones I've marked "Must read" first, and an end. Every morning at 6am, my Kindle gets one book of everything unread. I also was feeling nostalgic not to have a Sunday paper anymore so made a PDF export that you can print like a newspaper (as much as A4 paper size allows for)

Two things I only learned by using it myself:

The first morning's edition was great, until I realized that "it's on my Kindle" isn't the same as "I read it". So every chapter now ends with a "Mark as read" link that works from the Kindle's browser. The Kindle isn't logged in, so each link is HMAC-signed for its reader, and nothing is stored.

That first edition was also half paid-post teasers that stop at the paywall. Previews are now left out by default.

Things I cared about while building it: - Forwarding only. It never asks for Gmail access. - Tracking pixels are stripped when mail arrives. The site has no analytics and no third-party scripts. - Every page works with JavaScript off, and there's an eInk theme for Kobo, Boox and the Kindle browser. KOReader users get a private feed.

You can see what lands on the Kindle without signing up: https://newsstand.email/sample-edition

It also can be read directly on your phone and it was meant to be eInk tablet browser friendly in case you are accessing the page through a browser.

There is a paid tier but the free tier should cover most daily usage. Would love to get feedback!

story_text.value:
I've been building something and it's out today: status. It's all about breaking the ice. Keeping in touch takes more than it should. A full post feels like a performance, a message out of the blue needs a reason and sometimes it means saying something in a group chat. So post an emoji and a few words, and your people can react, reply or message you for a natter.

Everything has a status already: WhatsApp, Slack, Facebook. But there it sits on the side, something few people use in an app built for something else. I wanted it up front and centre.

It's a SvelteKit and Svelte 5 web app with a Fastify and PostgreSQL api. The iPhone and Android apps are Capacitor shells around the live site. Sign in by email link or passkey, no passwords. No ads and no tracking.

I built it with Claude. I write the requirements like ADRs, ai-dev-tasks turns them into a PRD and a task list, Claude Design draws it and Claude Code builds it with my own skills for design to code and for principles. My tip: pay attention. If you don't tell the robots how to behave and then check how they behaved, you'll get something you didn't ask for.

How and why I built it: https://feedmypixel.com/status

My skills: https://github.com/feedmypixel/principles

iPhone: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6829789500

Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=app.status.me

Have a play and let me know what you think.

story_text.value:
I made this Icon lib where it guides users through generating specific icons based on text description of icons in different styles (with AI) and then afterwards turning the image into Vector before the user can then choose to upload it to a pack, for everyone to use in their projects in the future

I found this idea interesting because most icon packs don't have all icons in them, but with AI we can sort of solve that. - The quality is not exactly near human created icons, but its a very good middle ground for when you need a few unique icons or are missing a few icons from your favorite pack!

Chameleon Icons is out and ready to try today! You can make Icons completely for free (without an account) and help fill in icons that are missing in your favorite packs (if you log in), or make a new pack based on a detailed description!

There is also a package on npm you can install so the icons can be used easily in code right after adding them to the platform!

Perhaps you are not building something right now where this could be useful, but maybe in your next project you are going to need a unique icon and then it might be useful to remember back on this post!

Anyways, hope you have a great day!

story_text.value:
My name is Aleksei Babkin, I am CEO and CTO of Aisma Video Editor project.

Main feature of Aisma is understanding of simple user request about editing of his video, and explain to generation model what exactly need to change, skipping parts where no need to change anything, decreasing the price of editing.

Aisma can work in any browsers, native iOS and Android apps, also API, MCP connection are available for comfortable work using AI agents and also our new goal is native ChatGPT plugin was reached, available in all markets where plugins in ChatGPT are available.

Main idea, as I told before, was to minimize price of editing by preview of video and apply each part of prompt to the part of video where it should to be edited, and even if some part was edited not perfectly, you will have an opportunity to add details and edit only this part of your video, which can be x10 times cheaper than new try to edit all video again and finally get issue in other part of result...

Now we support video from 2 to 60 seconds, but going to increase maximal length to 180 sec already at the beginning of 2027

All new users have a free credits which are enough for 10 sec video editing, but this is temporary promo, because as everyone knows this promo will be abused by many not polite users.

If you have any questions I will be here next several hours, also you can always reach me by email ceo@aisma.ai

story_text.value:
TL;DR:

- Free and open source, no seat limits.

  - Some of its features require plans that cost a team of 10 around $1,000/year on Clockify or $2,000/year on Toggl Track.
- No backend. Your time entries live in your private GitHub repo.

- Track any URL.

- Works offline, syncs in the background and keeps changes in Git history.

- Team reports, CSV exports, historical hourly rates, multiple currencies and PDF invoices, all in the browser.

Hi HN. I'm Sergey, one of the developers behind Manticore Search.

We'd been using Clockify for years until they decided to limit their free plan to five users recently. We started looking around. Being an open-source company, we weren't particularly excited about paying another monthly fee per employee. But we didn't want to self-host a server and a database for what is essentially a stopwatch either.

Then we thought: we already use GitHub for most of our work (dev, PM, CRM, CMS). Why not use it for time tracking too?

So we built Clockoli. Our whole team (Manticore Search) switched to it about a month ago, and so far it's been working well for us.

Each team member writes to their own branch. Even if we abandon Clockoli tomorrow, your synced data isn't going anywhere. Just git clone the repo and do whatever you want with it: look through the history, write your own scripts, let an AI agent analyze the data or even build your own tools around it.

There are downsides, of course. You depend on GitHub. Anyone with read access to the repo can see the team's time entries, so if you need to keep some of them private from your teammates, this might not be for you. Hourly rates, though, are stored in your browser and never committed to the repo.

It works for us, but I'm wondering if it would work for other teams too. Would you use something like this? If not, what would stop you?

title.value: Show HN: We replaced our time tracking SaaS with a Git repository

story_text.value:
BongBong is a fast-paced tank shooter game inspired by the NES tank shooters from 80's/90's that I used to play with my neighbour when I was a kid.

I wanted to give my kids the amazing feeling of building worlds - and then fighting in them. Keeping things "pixelated" but equally entertaining and realistic.

Geme is written in Rust and uses Raylib as the backbone, with the Rapier physics engine and HECS for ECS.

It is compiled to WASM for browsers and runs on iOS, macOS, Android, Windows and Linux. There is also a coop, so u can play with other friends across platforms.

I'm trying to polish it enough to release it to the Apple App Store, Google Play Store, and other stores.

It is not a "one-shot" game, but it is built using AI and agentic workflows. But most importantly, it is fun to play and to build.

Feedback appreciated!

story_text.value:
RCHIVE is a cross-platform desktop app for cataloging, searching and reorganizing files on your computers and drives. Like, all of 'em: internal, external, network shares, USB sticks, loose SD cards, weird CD-R's, DVDs, floppy disks, Zip disks, and everything in between.

I built this thing because my digital archives are an embarrassment! 30 years of getting a new hard drive whenever capacity quadrupled and dragging the old one to it into a folder titled "BACKUP - TO SORT" will do that to you lol, especially when you know deep down that "sorting" will never happen. To try to deal with that growing mess on a daily basis, I've tried a patchwork of all of our favorites in the past -- Everything, grep, custom scripts, you name it. And don't get me started on built-in OS defaults like Windows Explorer, Finder, Spotlight. I figured it was time to make something better-suited to my tastes, and 4200 commits later here we are!

RCHIVE scans as many different sources as you throw at it, gives you unified deep search across the entire catalog (with drives connected or disconnected), allows you to virtually organize and clean up giant archives of digital stuff by applying recipes and transformations, resiliently copies or moves files when you're ready to actually restructure on disk, or just lets you quickly pop in to find something or browse everything with previews, metadata, etc.

It works on Windows, Mac or Linux, works offline, has zero telemetry, deletes nothing, and is fully deterministic in operation. So, no wacky AI integrations for decision making or classification, everything is predictable and repeatable, you can even run portable versions off of a USB drive if you don't want to install it.

I've been using it all day every day for a year and am just stoked to have it out there, get some users, get some feedback (good or bad), and see what people think. There's a free trial, no email address or anything needed.

The website is also full of videos, features, comparisons, all that stuff, as well as a ncdu-like companion app for figuring out where the hell all your disk space went.

Anyways, check it out! Should come in handy if you're ever in Grand Central trying to find a garbage file left on some dude's Gibson.

https://www.rchive.computer

title.value: Show HN: Rchive – Every drive I've owned since the 90s, searchable in one window

story_text.value:
I put together a narrated map of the Texas Revolution. You can listen to a 20-minute audio guided version or just scroll through the events:

I thought the chronological and location based timeline made it easier to follow and learn as well. I was inspired by Mapbox’s “storytelling” template on GitHub and built my own version with MapLibre fork of Mapbox GL (with free satellite imagery and terrain tiles from USGS) and lots of help from Claude. There are lots of parameters that were built in, like the rotation and transition speed. Essentially themed it and added source links to the cards.

The information was sourced from Handbook of Texas by THC. The voice is AI generated using Elevenlabs v4. That github project https://github.com/mapbox/storytelling has some cool use-case examples that have been published as web features by a few publications. There is so much more you can do with this, like hooking it to live data. The template is a great place to start!

Narrations by Elevenlabs TTS.

Working on this new one around Houston Oil industry as well. https://whistlestop.guide/features/houston-oil

story_text.value: I love gaming but now in my 30's, there's never enough time and when I have an hour, I have no idea what to play or what I'll actually finish so I watch Youtube or buy more games I'll never play. I built UpNext so I can focus on the games I own and enjoy them. It takes in all your game libraries, play history and favorites. Simply tell it your mood and how much time you have and it suggests games. Every game gets details like length, review scores, what it feels like to play, what players say, and tags pulled from Steam, PCGamingWiki, ProtonDB, etc. Local and remote AI supported but not required. Available on Windows, Linux, Docker, Steam Deck (flatpak), Android APK. Runs locally with no accounts. Built in Rust and TypeScript with Opus 5.5, MIT/Apache 2.0 License Do you think the picks are still good with no AI?

title.value: Show HN: UpNext – Game backlog decider. Play what you own

story_text.value:
Hey HN!

It's Ved, the founder of Merget.

Merget is a GitHub App that connects to your code repositories and autonomously manages your PR queue using deep static analysis.

We can detect overlapping semantic relationships, order your queue in the most optimal order, and resolve merge conflicts in parallel across all of your PRs, ensuring your tests and CI continue to pass.

In short, you can advance main by dozens of PRs with a single click, safely :)

We hope to ease the burden of code produced by agentic workloads and save dev teams time and tokens! It's free to try.
